#9145. Photographer Can Take Jigsaw Puzzle Company to Court Over Use of His Photos

Photographer Can Take Jigsaw Puzzle Company to Court Over Use of His Photos

A photographer can proceed with his copyright infringement lawsuit against a Canadian puzzle-maker that allegedly used his images on its jigsaw puzzles.

Last week, a judge ruled that professional landscape and nature photographer Elliot McGucken could pursue copyright infringement and Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) claims against Canadian puzzle manufacturer Karmin International.

In his lawsuit, McGucken claims that Karmin International reproduced five of his photographs without authorization on its puzzles in its “Nature’s Beauty” series and placed their own copyright notices on the resulting products. The companies allegedly sold the puzzles across the United States, including in New York.

McGucken argues that this was misleading because the copyright notices suggested that Karmin International owned the rights to photographs that he had taken. He also alleges that the companies removed identifying and copyright information from his original images before reproducing them on the puzzles. McGucken alleges that the companies continued selling the products and displaying his photographs even after receiving notices from Shutterstock concerning the alleged infringement.

McGucken sued Karmin International, but the puzzle manufacturer asked the court to dismiss several of the photographer’s claims in his lawsuit. However, on November 3, Judge John G. Koeltl of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that the photographer could proceed with most of his copyright infringement claims against the puzzle maker.

According to Vital Law, Judge Koeltl ruled that McGucken had provided sufficient grounds for his allegations that Karmin International used false copyright notices on the jigsaw packaging and removed identifying information from his original photographs.

The judge also allowed McGucken’s claim of vicarious copyright infringement to proceed. This means a company can potentially be held responsible for another party’s copyright infringement if it has the ability to supervise the activity and benefits financially from it. McGucken alleges that Karmin and its marketing affiliate Playview worked together to produce and market the puzzles and that they both benefited from the sales.

Lyles & King presents new paintings by Kate Meissner in our project space, on view through April 4. Kate Meissner writes: "These works are an exploration of the human body's elasticity and capacity to metamorphose. Informed by my own experience of pregnancy and the birth of my first child last year, these paintings are a meditation on physiological transformation and the body's underlying animalistic and mammalian nature."

Kate Meissner (b. 1995, Sacramento, CA) lives and works in Los Angeles, CA. Her work is in the permanent collections of Denver Art Museum, Denver, CO; Xiao Museum of Contemporary Art, Rizhao, CN; The Mer Collection, Madrid, ES; and Abroms-Engel Institute for the Visual Arts, Birmingham, US. She received her MFA from Yale University. Meissner is represented by Lyles & King, New York.

#9143. Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

This Film Friday is featuring our favorite low-light film: Kodak T-Max P3200. T-Max P3200 is one of the fastest films you can load into your favorite 35mm camera and is perfect for a night out if the flash has to stay home or for just scratching that itch you have for superb contrast and graininess.

There are not many super-high-speed options out there in the film world. Ilford manufactures Delta 3200 (in both 35mm and 120, no less), and Kodak has T-Max P3200. Below that, you drop to ISO 800 in color and all the way to ISO 400 for the next fastest B&W film. Back in the day, we had Fujifilm Neopan 1600, Provia 1600, and Natura 1600, among a few other options, but those are long gone. So, the two 3200 films we have on the market fill an important role.

Kodak T-Max P3200 (TMZ for short) was originally introduced in 1988 as the third member of Kodak’s T-Max family of films, along with T-Max 100 (TMX) and T-Max 400 (TMY). The T-Max films are noteworthy for their T-grain structure. Similar to Ilford’s Delta films, T-grain films are designed to produce a smoother grain structure that has less grittiness to it and prints and scans more cleanly. But honestly, you will never think of T-Max P3200 as a fine-grained film—quite the opposite, in fact. But that’s OK, because its grain is one of the features we like best about it.

Let’s face it. T-Max P3200 is grainy, but grain is the price you will pay for speed. Our recommendation is to embrace grain, learn to appreciate it, and even love it. Grain is the building block of analog images; it is an integral part of how the photo is made. Once you come around to this, your love of black-and-white films will only grow and grow. And if you are already a fan of film grain, there are few films out there that will please you more than P3200. Buy this film for its grain and consider everything else it has to offer as icing on the cake.

Speaking of which, grain is not the only feature T-Max P3200 has going for it. Its other big strength is its speed. The film is marketed as an ISO 3200 film. If you do any sort of research into this film, you will quickly discover that it is really an ISO 800–1000 film (depending on how you develop it). The “P” in P3200 stands for “push”, as in that is what you are essentially doing with this film when shooting it at 3200.

Our suggestion? Forget all of that. It just causes confusion. Think of P3200 as an ISO 3200 film, because among the many things it does well is expose at ISO 3200. Rate this film at its box speed, go out into the dark, and odds will be good that you come home with decent exposures. This reliability at high speeds has long endeared T-Max P3200 to us. In contrast, while there are things we like about Ilford Delta 3200, we almost never expose it at ISO 3200, generally opting for a slower ISO 1600 or even ISO 1000 rating to help ensure decent exposures. In our experience, Delta 3200 needs to be paired with Ilford developers to really hold onto its speed, whereas P3200 doesn’t seem to be quite as picky. With T-Max P3200, we have no fear of rating it for those higher speeds.

And speaking of higher speeds, T-Max P3200 can actually go even higher. One of our own staff members set out on a mission to see how high he could take P3200. He got it up to ISO 102,400 before he felt like the process (either the film’s sensitivity or his developing) was breaking down. While his results at those absurdly high speeds are grainy beyond belief and have crunched shadows, they do an excellent job of showing the versatility of this film. Even if ISO 102,400 is not your cup of tea, rest assured that the film will handle ISO 6400 or 12800 pretty dang well.

So, you have grain and speed. The third element we love about P3200 is its contrast. T-Max P3200 has dramatic contrast. It is an atmospheric film. Pair it with dramatic light, and the results will be eye-catching. The shadows and highlights on P3200 tend to go toward the extreme, with the shadows getting crunchy and the highlights slipping into bleached white. In good hands, these qualities make for great images; just be mindful that, if the highlights or shadows are important to you, you should meter the image accordingly.

If you have stuck around this long, we’ll treat you to a little historical “bet you didn’t know”. If you have ever wondered why Kodak has never manufactured this emulsion in medium format, well… they did. They actually tried to make P3200 in 120 but ran into technical issues they could not fix.

Apparently, the emulsion of P3200 is so sensitive that the slight lip from where the tape connects the film to the backing paper was causing a slight pressure mark in the first frame. Kodak couldn’t eliminate it and figured they couldn’t market the film as an “11 exposure” roll film, so the idea got axed. But still, thinking about shooting P3200 in 120 keeps us awake some nights considering the possibilities.

So, that is our review of T-Max P3200. It is a film we use when we know we need the speed (low light). Or when we have an itch for grain and grit (texture). Or when we are hoping for a bit more contrast in our images (drama). We love T-Max P3200 and were heartbroken when Kodak discontinued it in 2012, and we were likewise elated when it was reintroduced in 2018. T-Max P3200 was given a reprieve from death, and all of us film photographers have benefited from its returning to the market. So make sure you have taken the chance to try a roll of it.

Hit up Blue Moon’s website via the link or visit our Portland, Oregon-based shop to enjoy a Film Friday discount on this wonderful film. Today only!

#9142. Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh

Self-portraits by the Bloomsbury painters: Vanessa Bell (around 1915) and Duncan Grant (detail) (around 1920)

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.

Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.

As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing new and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”

Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.

As so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.

Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.

The Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.

It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

The impact of Post-Impressionism: Duncan Grant's The Mantelpiece (1914) and Vanessa Bell's Still Life on Corner of a Mantelpiece (1914)

Grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s New Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.

The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.

Van Gogh’s Bouquet of Flowers (summer 1886)

private collection (formerly Galerie Schmit, Paris)

But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.

This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a new life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”

Catalogue of the second Post-Impressionist catalogue (1912), co-designed by Bell, Grant and Fry

Bibliothèque de l'Institut National d'Histoire de l'Art, Jacques Doucet collections

In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.

Bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.

How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.

The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).

In 1911, the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.

Decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

#9141. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#9140. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

There are a number of reasons a new or old tattoo can itch. Infections, allergic reactions, and preexisting skin conditions are just a few possible…

#9139. I Spent Four Days With the Leica Q3 43 F1 Camera

I Spent Four Days With the Leica Q3 43 F1 Camera

Formula One has changed a lot since I’ve been watching. People used to look at me strangely when I said I enjoyed watching race cars drive around in circles on a Sunday. Now, the sport is swamped by new fans drawn to the sport via Netflix’s Drive to Survive and Charles Leclerc’s boyish good looks.

I hold no ill will towards this new generation of fans who I doubt can list every F1 World Champion going all the way back to the 1980s as I can. In fact, without them, I dare say I would never have received the limited edition Leica Q3 43 F1 edition in a brown cardboard box this week.

After news broke about the new camera, I simply had to try it. Photography and F1 have a history: Canon sponsored Williams in the team’s glory days; possibly my favourite F1 photo of all time is Nigel Mansell and Ayrton Senna glancing over at each other while driving almost 200 miles per hour in Barcelona in 1991. Their wheels are inches apart from each other, both daring each other to see who will brake first. The sponsor on Mansell’s wing reads ‘Canon.’

So far as I know, this is Leica’s first-ever foray into F1. The special version of the Q3 43 comes with carbon fiber grips, a material that’s both light and strong, which is why F1 teams have been using it to build cars for the past 40 years.

The camera comes covered in non-slip microvelour that’s modeled on a racing steering wheel. The pictures really don’t do this material justice; it’s a beautiful touch and I couldn’t stop running my fingers over it, like when you’ve just shaved your head.

That’s not all the F1-inspired hardware, either. The shutter is a soft-release button with a carbon inlay and red rim. It reminds me of an old-school stopwatch, the kind you’d see in a movie about a promising young rookie arriving for testing with an established team at a rain-soaked racetrack somewhere in England. He completes his first lap, the timekeeper clicks the stopwatch, glances at the time, turns to the engineers, and gives a knowing smile. You just know he’s going to be something special.

Having never shot a Leica Q3 of any focal length, I immediately fell in love with it. I mean, it’s just so damn beautiful. It’s a perfectly proportioned camera, and a joy to use. It took me no time at all to set up, and I particularly enjoyed the little ‘zoom’ button that crops into the sensor from the 60-megapixel 43mm to the five-megapixel 150mm end.

And it’s certainly a head-turner. I showed it to as many people as I could over the past four days, and everyone was taken with it. The BMXers were particularly impressed with the microvelour finish. My mom called it “handsome.”

I wanted to shoot some pulsating auto action with it, but I quickly realized that — despite the F1 logo on the front — it’s not exactly a camera for shooting high-speed objects. It’s still a Leica Q3; it’s a camera that wants you to slow down and think carefully about what you’re shooting. In his review of the Q3 43, Chris Niccolls said, “There is a simplicity and a meditative experience to be had, wandering the streets with a compact camera on your shoulder.” That is true.

As I write this, the camera is already on its way back to Leica. I will miss it. But at almost $10,000, it’s very unlikely I will be buying one.

#9138. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9136. How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

Wildlife photography is about more than finding an animal and capturing a sharp image. Understanding animal behavior helps photographers anticipate movement, recognize meaningful interactions, and capture moments that reveal more about a subject than its appearance alone—they tell a story.

Most of all, taking the time before you even pick up your camera to learn how to read body language and recognize behavioral patterns can make the difference between reacting to an action and being ready when it happens.

A photograph can show an animal in beautiful detail, but behavior gives the image another layer of meaning and wow factor. The way an animal moves, feeds, communicates, interacts with others, or responds to its surroundings offers insight into its daily life. Capturing these moments helps tell a more complete story and gives viewers a better sense of the animal beyond its physical appearance.

Behavior also creates opportunities for more compelling compositions. An animal looking directly toward the camera can make an effective portrait, but a photograph of it displaying, feeding, preening, or interacting with another animal can communicate much more. These moments introduce action and context, giving the viewer something to interpret rather than simply observe.

Understanding behavior is particularly valuable because some of the most powerful wildlife photography sits at the intersection of storytelling and documentation of animals’ lives. Animals follow routines and respond to their surroundings according to instinct, environmental conditions, and social relationships. Photographers who recognize these patterns have a better chance of anticipating what might happen next and preparing to capture it.

One of the best ways to become a more effective wildlife photographer is to spend time learning about the animals you want to photograph before heading into the field. Wildlife documentaries, online videos, books, scientific articles, and species-specific resources can all provide useful information about feeding habits, courtship, territorial displays, migration, nesting, and other behaviors. Watching footage can be especially helpful because it allows photographers to see how an animal moves and how one action often leads to another.

However, learning does not have to happen entirely through research. Spending time observing animals in person is just as important, particularly when you can return to the same location regularly. Birds are a common and effective starting point because they are found in a wide range of environments and display an extensive variety of behaviors. Even a local park can offer opportunities to learn how different species feed, interact, defend territory, and respond to people or other animals. To keep things simple, I will focus primarily on birds throughout this article, as their visibility and varied habits make them ideal subjects for study.

When first learning about wildlife photography and animal behavior, simply sitting on a park bench with a book while casually observing nearby birds can be a useful exercise. Watch how they move through their environment, how often they pause to look around, and what they do before taking flight. Notice how their behavior changes when another bird approaches or when people move nearby. With repeated observation, familiar actions become easier to recognize, and you begin to notice patterns that might otherwise go overlooked.

Locations where large numbers of birds gather can be particularly valuable places to practice. For me, rookeries along the New Jersey shore provide opportunities to observe nesting activity, courtship, feeding, and interactions among birds. During winter, the gathering of bald eagles around Conowingo Dam in Maryland offers a chance to watch feeding behavior, competition, and interactions around fish. Areas of open water that attract wintering ducks and geese, including snow geese, are also useful observation sites. When many birds gather in one location, photographers can watch different behaviors happening simultaneously and compare how individual species respond to one another.

To find wildlife hotspots near you, research is key. Look up local Audubon chapters, birding groups, and guided trips—whether on social media or through organized photo walks at nature centers. These communities can be a great source of camaraderie, education, and field assistance.

The goal at these hotspots should be to observe just as much as to photograph. Rather than immediately concentrating on getting a particular image, spend time watching the birds and learning what is happening around you. Notice where they tend to gather, when activity increases, and how they respond to changes in their surroundings. Most of all, returning to the same location can reveal patterns that are difficult to recognize during a single visit.

Animals communicate through more than vocalizations. Posture, movement, positioning, and subtle changes in appearance can all provide clues about what an animal is doing or how it is responding to something nearby. Learning to recognize these signals helps photographers distinguish ordinary activity from moments that may lead to an interesting interaction or display.

Birds provide many visible examples. Changes in posture, feather position, head movements, and wing displays can indicate courtship, aggression, alertness, or preparation for flight. A bird that repeatedly looks in one direction may be responding to another animal or monitoring a potential threat. A change in stance or a sudden pause can also signal that its attention has shifted.

Recognizing these signals also gives photographers time to prepare their camera settings. If a bird begins shifting its weight, lowering its body, or opening its wings before taking flight, it may be time to increase the shutter speed and switch to a continuous autofocus mode if you are not already using one. If two birds begin displaying toward each other, consider widening the composition and checking that your shutter speed is fast enough to freeze sudden movement. Small adjustments made before the action begins can make a significant difference.

Hunting herons and egrets are great subjects to practice on, as they methodically scour shallow water to snatch up prey. This predictable, repetitive behavior gives you time to observe, learn, and test your own “hunting” skills.

Once photographers become familiar with an animal’s routines, they can begin anticipating what it may do next. Many wildlife behaviors follow recognizable sequences, even though the exact timing can vary. An animal may pause before moving, shift its posture before taking flight, or display a series of movements before interacting with another individual. Recognizing these patterns creates opportunities to prepare for the photograph rather than simply reacting after the action begins.

Camera settings should reflect the behavior you expect to photograph. For a stationary bird or mammal, a shutter speed around 1/500 second is often a useful starting point, although the appropriate speed depends on the focal length, subject movement, and camera stability. For walking animals or birds that are moving more quickly, 1/1000 second can provide a better chance of freezing motion. Takeoff, flight, running, and fast interactions may require 1/2000 second or faster, particularly when you want to preserve detail in wings or other rapidly moving parts.

For example, when photographing eagles gathering around a feeding area, a bird preening on a branch may be relatively easy to capture at 1/1000 second. However, if you are anticipating a takeoff or an interaction over a fish, increasing the shutter speed to 1/2000 or 1/3200 second can help freeze the action. Birds in flight against a relatively clear background may also be easier to track with continuous autofocus and subject recognition enabled, depending on the camera system.

Aperture is another important consideration. When photographing a single animal, a wide aperture such as f/4 or f/5.6 can help separate the subject from a distracting background while allowing more light to reach the sensor. However, when photographing two animals interacting, a slightly narrower aperture may provide enough depth of field to keep both subjects sharp, particularly if they are not positioned on the same focal plane. The trade-off is that a smaller aperture may require a higher ISO or slower shutter speed.

Auto ISO can be useful when photographing unpredictable behavior. Setting a minimum shutter speed and allowing the camera to adjust ISO as light changes can help maintain the speed needed to freeze movement. In rapidly changing conditions, this can be more practical than trying to adjust exposure manually while following an animal. It is still worth keeping an eye on the ISO, especially in low light, to avoid introducing more noise than necessary.

Another useful option is to configure a custom camera button or shooting mode for unexpected action. I set up what I call an “oh heck” setting, which switches my camera to its widest available aperture, a shutter speed of 1/2000 second, continuous autofocus, and burst shooting. When an animal suddenly takes off, starts fighting, or begins an interaction, I can press one button and have the camera ready for action without having to change several settings while the moment is unfolding. Many cameras offer customizable buttons or saved shooting modes that can be configured in a similar way. The exact settings can be adjusted to suit your camera, the subjects you photograph, and the conditions you typically work in, but having a ready-to-go action setup can make a real difference when something happens without warning.

Autofocus settings should also reflect the situation. Continuous autofocus, often called AF-C or AI Servo depending on the camera manufacturer, is generally the better choice when an animal is moving or likely to move. Animal subject detection can help maintain focus as the subject changes position, while a suitable tracking area gives the camera enough flexibility to follow its movement. For a stationary animal, a smaller focus area may offer more precise control, especially when branches, reeds, or other foreground elements could interfere with subject detection.

Composition needs to account for movement as well. If you expect an animal to take off, leave room in front of it rather than placing it tightly against the edge of the frame. When photographing feeding or social interactions, a slightly wider composition can preserve the surrounding context and keep important parts of the action from being cropped out. You can always refine the composition later, provided the original file retains enough resolution.

Anticipation also requires flexibility. Wildlife does not always follow predictable patterns, and an animal may change direction or abandon an activity without warning. Avoid becoming so committed to one expected moment that you miss something else happening nearby. Keep observing the entire scene, even when you are focused on a particular subject.

Some of the most engaging wildlife photographs involve more than one animal. Social interactions can reveal communication, cooperation, competition, courtship, and relationships between parents and young. These moments often provide a stronger sense of the animals’ lives than an isolated portrait because the photograph captures a relationship or exchange.

Photographing interactions requires paying attention to more than one subject. Watch how animals position themselves in relation to each other, how they respond to movement, and whether an encounter is developing into a larger display. The most meaningful part of an interaction may happen quickly, so it helps to anticipate the sequence rather than concentrate exclusively on a single frame.

Camera settings can become more challenging when multiple animals are involved. If two birds are interacting at close range, a shutter speed of 1/1600 to 1/2500 second can help freeze sudden movements, while an aperture around f/5.6 or f/8 may provide more depth of field than shooting wide open. The exact combination depends on the available light and how far apart the subjects are. If one animal is closer to the camera than the other, even f/8 may not provide enough depth of field to keep both sharp, so consider your shooting angle and focus placement as well.

Autofocus can also be less predictable when animals overlap or move across one another. A camera may switch focus between subjects, particularly when they are close together. If subject detection struggles, adjusting the autofocus area or using a more controlled tracking zone can help. Keeping a little extra room around the interaction also gives you flexibility if the animals move unexpectedly.

It is worth watching what happens after an apparent interaction ends. Animals may continue communicating, move together, or return to a familiar routine. Staying attentive beyond the most obvious action can lead to photographs that reveal more about the relationship between the subjects.

Knowing what is typical for a species helps photographers recognize when something worth capturing is about to happen. Familiarity with everyday routines makes changes in activity easier to notice, whether that means an interaction, a shift to feeding behavior, or a response to changing environmental conditions. Learning about the species and observing it over time provides a more reliable basis for understanding what is happening.

One example that I often use in my work is that ducks preening in the water often dunk their heads, shake, and then flap their wings to dry off. Knowing this sequence allows me to capture a signature “angel wing” pose time and time again across various species.

Developing an understanding of wildlife behavior takes time. A single outing may provide a few useful observations, but returning to the same locations allows photographers to build a more complete picture of an animal’s routines. Seasonal changes can also influence behavior, making familiar locations worth revisiting throughout the year.

Repeated observation helps photographers become more selective. Instead of photographing every movement, they begin to recognize which moments are likely to produce meaningful images. They may also become more familiar with the best times and locations for observing particular activities, making future outings more productive.

For example, while photographing screech owls, I have often found them resting in tree cavities during the day, but the real action and behavior of these nocturnal predators are best photographed at dusk.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Patience is an important part of this process. Not every visit will result in a memorable photograph, and some of the most useful outings may involve spending more time watching than shooting. That time is still valuable. It builds familiarity with the animals and makes it easier to recognize opportunities when they arise.

Above all, respect for wildlife should remain central to every outing. Maintain appropriate distances, follow local guidelines, and avoid disturbing animals around nesting, feeding, or resting areas. The objective is to document natural behavior, not change it.

Understanding wildlife behavior changes the way photographers approach their subjects. Instead of concentrating only on finding an animal and achieving a technically successful exposure, they begin paying attention to routines, body language, and the relationships between individuals and their surroundings.

The knowledge gained through research and repeated observation makes it easier to anticipate meaningful moments and prepare for them. Whether watching birds at a neighborhood park or spending time at a seasonal gathering, photographers can develop these skills without traveling far from home.

The strongest wildlife photographs go beyond showing what an animal looks like — they capture a glimpse of how it lives. By learning to read behavioral cues, anticipating action, and approaching every subject with patience and respect, photographers can turn fleeting encounters into compelling stories.

#9135. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#9134. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.
