#9056. Oshinówò Studio tops Lutyens-designed war memorial with glass prism to honour Sierra Leone's Carrier Corps

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission has unveiled a memorial to the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Officially opened this weekend, the memorial designed by Oshinówò Studio sits on top of a war memorial designed by British architect Edwin Lutyens in 1931.

While the original memorial honoured soldiers who died in the first world war, it did not include the names of the 946 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps – men enlisted to transport supplies and materials – who also died in the war.

Oshinówò Studio extended the Lutyens-designed, stone memorial by adding a structural glass pyramid etched with the names of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps men.

“The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts,” said Oshinówò Studio founder Tosin Oshinówò.

“The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens’ existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. “

According to Oshinówò, placing the names of the carrier corps men higher than the soldiers was also a symbolic move.

“In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served,” she said.

“There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today.”

Along with the glass pyramid, the memorial also includes a laser beacon that will be illuminated on significant days of remembrance. According to the team, this column of light will be visible from up to five kilometres.

As part of the project, the 1930s memorial was also full restored by stonemasons and bronze specialists from the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

Recent memorials featured on Dezeen include a “serene and contemplative” memorial to Queen Elizabeth II designed by Foster + Partners and a park in Ethiopia dedicated to the 157 victims of the Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash.

#9055. Prusa CORE One+ review: Built to last and grow with you

Prusa’s CORE One+ is a sturdy workhorse for makers who value fuss-free precision and ingenious engineering. It's not the fanciest machine on the market, in fact it's down right old school, but that is a feature, not a bug. After a year in my studio, its brilliantly simple design really stands out. Fewer parts equal fewer failures, but if things do go sidewise, I know that 24-7 tech help is at my fingertips.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

The CORE One+ is an enclosed Core XY 3D printer you can truly own, mod and repair, which has long been the cornerstone of Prusa Research. It goes toe to toe with Bambu Lab’s mid-sized machines, but its $1,299/£1,199 price tag makes it a more serious investment.

I’ve reviewed the best 3D printers since 2021, and Prusa’s concern for their customers has always stood out. I’ve had this CORE One for well over a year, and when the “Gen 2 +” came out, my machine wasn’t obsolete, it just needed a small bag of parts and a screwdriver.

The CORE One+ is the same size as the Original Prusa MK4S and can be upgraded into a multicolour master with an INDX tool changer upgrade.

We unboxed a fully assembled CORE One (which was later upgraded to a “+”). You only need to remove the packing material and install the screen. The machine arrives pre-calibrated from the factory so all you need to do is load filament and select your first print. The machine automatically probes the bed level before each print to ensure a perfect first layer.

The CORE One is made with a solid steel exoskeleton that also forms the machine’s chassis, and the print bed is milled aluminum for even heat distribution. Nothing on the machine is glued, and the entire thing can be taken apart with a screwdriver. This is to facilitate both repair and custom modding, which Prusa fully supports.

The 3D printer came with a set of tools, alcohol wipes, a detailed paper manual, a USB stick loaded with pre-sliced test prints and a full sized spool of Galaxy Black Prusament. You also get a bag of Haribo Goldbears to fuel your journey.

The CORE One+ is much faster than its bed slinger brethren, but honestly it's not as fast as a Bambu Lab X1C. This “space marine” phone holder I printed for my son (above) in Prusament PLA Pearl Mouse took 12 hours and 18 minutes to print, using a high quality .15mm layer height, 15% infill and 3 walls. An X1C would cut that down by 3 hours using similar settings. This is because PrusaSlicer, Prusa’s native slicing software, is optimized for precision rather than raw speed. Though both the CORE One+ and X1C are similar sized Core XY printers, Prusa never pushes the speed or travel settings on its machines.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The Prusa Nextruder is at the heart of the CORE One+, with its large planetary gear to firmly grab and control filament. Squirrely TPU is no match for the CORE One+, with a redesigned filament loading point that has a manual switch to loosen the sensor and allow soft TPU to slip through.

One of the best features given to the CORE One after its “+” upgrade is the simplest: a nozzle wiping brush. The small silicone brush started as a community mod, with dozens of variations uploaded to Printables. The printer can now clean its own nozzle before performing bed leveling probes, eliminating an annoying failure point.

One sticking point is the lack of a dedicated heater for the chamber. The CORE One+ depends on retaining heat generated by the heated bed, which can leave you waiting when you need a toasty interior for nylon or PC.

Prusa Research’s ecosystem consists of PrusaSlicer, PRUSA App for mobile and Printables.com for community file sharing. Printables hosts frequent contests, free models but also supports designers financially by allowing them to set up club memberships and shops.

EasySlice is a simple, yet fully functional, web based slicer you can run from the PRUSA App or directly from Printables. Prusa makes its own filament, Prusament, in house at both its headquarters in Prague and the more recently acquired Delaware factory, formally known as Printed Solid.

The Prusa CORE One+ typically retails $1,299/£1,199 assembled or $999/£929 for a kit, which is on the high end for an enclosed Core XY 3D printer. The company is currently running a Black Friday sale with free shipping and gifts worth up to $450. Gifts include an Open Print Tag upgrade, a spool of Chalky Blue PLA, premium models, Prusa Academy courses, and extended one year warranty, and $50 off an INDX upgrade.

The CORE One+ is definitely an investment, but the machine is built to last and carries the promise of years of upgrades. If you’re willing to do the occasional mod, this printer will likely serve you for years without getting kicked to the curb just because a new sensor package has come along. Fun fact: if you owned a MK2 ten years ago, you could have upgraded it all the way to a CORE One+.

For a bit less than an assembled CORE One+, you could get a Bambu Lab H2S Combo, a single nozzle 3D Core XY with a larger 340 x 320mm print bed and a four color AMS. The H2S is currently on sale for $1249/£999. We reviewed the laser variant, which is slightly more at $1599/£1249 and tops our list of Best 3D Printers.

You could also opt for a more modest machine, like the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo, which is closer in size with a 256x256mm build plate, but a fraction of the cost at $449/£398. It’s an enclosed four color Core XY, with good quality, though a bit lacking in the polished ecosystem of its rivals.

Buy it if: You’re a hobbyist who wants a machine you can maintain and mod yourself for years to come.

Don’t buy it if: You’re looking to print large models like cosplay armor.

Prusa’s CORE One+ is for hands-on makers who’ve outgrown bed slingers and crave a no nonsense, fully enclosed machine they can mod and repair. After more than a year with this machine in my studio, this is where it earns its keep. I personally enjoy its old-school vibe, and the thought that when things go wrong, I can sort it out with a screwdriver and mod from the community over at Printables. I’m already eyeballing an eight color INDX upgrade for this machine.

It's also an excellent fit for classrooms and workshops where people need a reliable, well-built machine that can handle a bit of benign neglect. Its enclosure means it can churn out high temperature filaments, like ASA and ABS, and its precision is a must have for practical prints and designing prototypes.

Denise is a tech reviewer, content creator, and former newspaper reporter with over 20 years of journalism experience. She's tested well over one hundred 3D printers and lasers for Tom's Hardware, and has traveled the world looking for the best tech to share with her readers. You're most likely to find her at a maker festival with her 3D printed RC Death Racer, The Harley Quinn.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Yes. Globalist elite status works at all Park Hyatt properties and unlocks suite upgrades (subject to availability), free breakfast, late checkout, and waived resort fees. This dramatically increases the total value of a points stay.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#9053. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#9052. EBBA Architects transforms former agricultural barn in Cornwall into a "calm sanctuary"

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.

Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.

EBBA Architects looked to restore the Dutch barn‘s original, open spatial character, expanding its area by almost a third with the addition of a pavilion-like extension that is framed by columns of white stone.

“The overall concept was about finding clarity in the form of the building and finding ways to add in a way that didn’t take away from the original character,” EBBA’s founding director, Benni Allan told Dezeen.

“Over the years the barn had gathered a series of piecemeal alterations that took away from the original simplicity. Our process involved removing later additions and then adding where felt most appropriate,” he added.

“The house is a place that will act as a place to enjoy the vast contrast of weather throughout the year, while also providing a calm sanctuary and background for family life.”

The ground-floor plan of Dutch Barn is based on the central position of an existing stair, around which a bathroom and storage core has been built to separate the more open kitchen and living spaces.

A row of full-height openings links the existing barn to its extension, where a long, uninterrupted space containing a skylit dining area and lounge opens out onto a covered colonnade via sliding doors.

“The intention is for the house to be used by the large family, and for there to be a blend between spaces,” Allan explained.

“We are always interested in making flexible arrangements in planform, to accommodate different ways of living.”

The home’s interior finishes were also guided by ideas of simplification, with plaster walls, concrete floors and gridded white-painted timber ceilings.

EBBA Architects wanted to emphasise material junctions, as seen in a new oak column in the kitchen, which has been rotated to highlight where it meets the flitch plates that connect it to the exposed ceiling beams.

Externally, this theme was extended into the design of the extension’s roof, which stops short of the edge of the stone columns to emphasise the point where the two meet.

The existing barn was clad in reused cedar shingles that were replaced where necessary, while the extension was built using white stone masonry that references the walls on the adjacent street.

“At first glance the house presents itself as a simple barn, but we like that a series of quite serious architectural moves have been complemented with some playful elements, such as the exaggeration of the junctions and the contrast between textured columns and clear, almost gallery-like floors,” explained Allan.

“We wanted the projecting roof and new columns to read as an independent object that reaches out into the garden and takes up the change in level, rather than as a continuation of the barn,” he added.

EBBA Architects has previously completed a cafe in Marylebone with clay plaster walls and an illuminated glass ceiling, and an apartment in London for its founder that is lined with Douglas fir.

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

#9051. vincent leroy installs kinetic cloud wireframe in morocco’s desert

building upon previous molecular cloud series, the project transforms the cloud-like volume into an open metal lattice, where lines and voids become inseparable.

Vincent Leroy edited by christina vergopoulou November 12, 2026 3 min

Sited in Morocco’s Agafay Desert, Molecular Cloud Wireframe is a kinetic installation by French artist Vincent Leroy that investigates spatial perception, movement, and structural transparency. Building upon his previous Molecular Cloud series, including the installation presented at Coachella, the project translates a cloud-like volume into an open, three-dimensional metal lattice where linear elements and empty voids share equal structural weight.

The interwoven metal framework outlines a constellation of intersecting spherical geometries through curved linear ribs. This porous configuration functions similarly to a three-dimensional moucharabieh, filtering sightlines and fragmenting views of the surrounding desert terrain as the viewer changes perspective. By dematerializing volume into a network of lines, the sculpture by artist Vincent Leroy operates simultaneously as a physical object and a spatial drawing. Diurnal shifts in natural light continually alter this reading: direct daylight emphasizes the structural depth and overlapping spherical volumes, while dusk increases contrast against the sky, flattening the three-dimensional assembly into a graphic, two-dimensional silhouette.

the semi-transparent metal cloud merges with the heavy, cloud-filled skiesin constant motion, the cloud shifts between fluidity and form

Voters have rejected data centres, and Nvidia’s CEO has resigned. If the AI honeymoon is over, what happens to creatives?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Until recently, the AI industry seemed unstoppable. Every week saw more powerful models, extra billions in funding, and a further spread of data centres. Anyone who complained was told: "Don't even bother. This is happening, whether you like it or not."

This month, though, things felt different. US voters delivered a blunt verdict on AI infrastructure in ballot measures, while Nvidia, the chipmaker who's played a vital role in building that infrastructure (and made RAM more expensive in the process), found itself at the centre of a spy scandal. The recent Nvidia scandal and resignation of Jensen Huang have sent things into a spiral, from a share price drop to speculation that the AI bubble has burst, even a rebranding, when we asked whether Nvidia need a new logo as well as a new CEO?

Neither story on its own spells disaster for AI. But together, they suggest something important has shifted. And that matters for the millions of creatives whose lives are being reshaped by this tech.

Most news coverage of the US midterms focused on who controls Congress. But at the same time, 40 of 41 local data centre measures decided on 3 November across 10 states favoured limiting development.

Voters approved 27 restrictive measures and rejected all 13 that would have helped projects go ahead. The results range from moratoriums and zoning limits to outright bans. And candidates who campaigned on pausing data centre construction won governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. This was not surprising, because in NBC News' exit poll, 76% of voters said they'd oppose a new data centre in their own community.

It's important to understand that this is not a partisan issue. Democrats, Republicans and Independents alike have been fighting back against the AI industry. So the timing couldn't have been worse for Nvidia.

On 6 November, The New York Times shared details of how CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of an alleged espionage operation involving a Chinese businesswoman US officials believe was working for China's Ministry of State Security. On Sunday, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with her and apologised to staff.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Huang said he had no idea she was a spy, and Beijing has dismissed the claims as groundless. Nvidia's board launched an inquiry and said it still had confidence in him. But later revelations of a second affair piled on the pressure, and Huang eventually resigned on 12 November.

Maybe I'm overreacting, but this feels like a watershed moment. Up until now, the AI industry has relied on two things: the assumption that its physical expansion was inevitable, and the aura of its leaders as visionaries above scrutiny. Now, that's changed.

That doesn't mean the AI boom is about to collapse, of course. But it does suggest the era of 'build first, ask questions later' is ending. Expect more political resistance, more regulation and more scrutiny.

For creatives, that may be a double-edged sword. On the one hand, if you're using AI tools, they're likely to go up in price. On the other hand, if you're worried about AI's impact on jobs and don't want it to scrape your work, there's a chance things will slow down now, at least a little.

Finally, it feels like a good time to remember that we actually have a voice. For years now, many of us have either kept quiet or felt like we've been shouting into the void about AI. Now that millions of voters are shouting too, the industry might actually start to pay attention.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). #9049. Carsten Höller installs "largest" of his slides in Mexico City

Artist Carsten Höller has installed the largest-ever version of his architectural slides as part of a development in Mexico City led by local architecture studio Sordo Madaleno.

Mexico City Slides is Höller‘s latest slide installation yet and features four slides ranging from 12 to 38 meters in height and 31 to 90 meters in length.

The metallic slides with transparent sections cascade around the courtyard of the Antara development in Mexico City’s Polanco neighbourhood, a joint venture between architecture studio Sordo Madaleno and its development arm, SOMA.

It is part of the wider Colonia Granada district.

“Mexico City Slides, which is my largest project with slides so far, connects four different parts of the buildings that make up the new Antara destination,” said Höller.

Its courtyard location, curated by Arte Abierto, is between several buildings containing retail and offices, including an office for technology company Google. A 43-storey tower for a Mexico City Rosewood Hotel is also planned for the site.

The slides take people from various parts of the retail, hospitality and office programming down to a central outdoor landing area.

Höller emphasised the slides’ role in taking people out of their usual routine through a combination of “joy and fear”.

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants and from an art centre are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” said Höller.

“They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”

Höller continued, calling the slides “an existential experience of bare life, not unlike a ‘voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind'”.

The artist has designed multiple of these slides across the world. These include installations in a Florentine palazzo, woven through the Anish Kapoor-designed ArcelorMittal Orbit in London and, with a tower, at Vitra campus.

Yoto is winning the low-screen moment by holding back. Its designers explain how they balanced a vocal community with a clear mission.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve been obsessed with Yoto since 2019, when a friend introduced me to the tactile, lo-fi audio player for kids. My children have used it daily ever since, and it’s one of the most interesting brands out there. It arrived just as parents were looking for an alternative to endless high-stimulation screens, and it has grown from a community-led, Kickstarter-style product with its foibles into a polished, self-assured brand that still listens closely to its community.

So when I heard a new generation was on its way, I asked to speak to the design team behind the biggest shake-up of its physical design yet. It’s a fairly tricky proposition: a product used by children but invested in by parents, with a clear mission and a feature set that’s still evolving. The new players have a mischievous new look, a green dial (big news in the world of Yoto) and a few other added features. Most importantly, the design team and Yoto chose not to lean any harder on the screen’s capabilities. For families trying to rely less on screens, that’s a crucial decision.

Below is my conversation with Jack Godfrey Wood of design studio Heirloom, covering the design mission, how the players were prototyped and tested, and the challenge of designing for a product with such a clear purpose and such a vocal community.

We knew people there. One of our colleagues worked on the original Kickstarter version, the wooden cube with the two blue dials, and two of our team designed the later generations at another company. When we started Heirloom, we took on the current fourth-gen players, so our team has been involved in and out from the beginning. It made sense straight away, because we all had that Fisher-Price cassette deck as kids and this felt like this generation’s version. Once Tom and Ben showed us the community they’d built, I knew it would work.

There were technical aims and design aims. Yoto wanted more storage, more battery and more internal robustness, and they wanted the player to be splashproof. That meant a lot of work on keeping dust and liquid out. Inside, the downloads are faster, there’s more storage and the sound is better, so they’ve fixed the things I wanted fixed as a parent. Our job was to make the players fit better in kids’ hands, travel better, and be easier to hold, carry and drop without anything breaking.

Sign up to the design newsletter from Creative Bloq, brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of graphic design, branding, typography and more.

Where did your design decisions come from?

Both the community and our own experience, plus writing some rules. Yoto’s core goal is “kids in control and parents in charge”. We also knew we didn’t want addictive, distracting moments. Both screens have more resolution than before, but we kept everything in pixel world, because to us that’s Yoto. It’s a fun menu, not a distracting screen. We could have added motion, like a character that waves at you if nothing happens for 15 minutes, but we felt the community would say that was wrong.

Does Yoto’s approach feel different to other consumer tech clients?

Yes. Yoto’s goal isn’t to keep eyeballs on the screen. It’s how often the player gets used and whether it adds value to a child’s and a family’s life. It’s a very clear moral code, which makes design decisions easier. A lot of the pixel work we did is artful, precise and beautiful, but we kept it happily lo-fi and didn’t turn it into another Apple product.

Yoto wanted the backup content stored in each player to be available on the player itself. That way, if you can’t find the card, your kids can still listen to what they like, and you don’t have to get your phone out at 9pm when nobody’s going to bed. The hard part was doing that without turning the screen into an iPod or an iPad.

It was our way of giving kids access to what they want without overwhelming them with 200 cards. Daily radio and podcasts have moved onto it, along with 20 favourites. It populates automatically, but parents can set up day and night versions in the app. At night, all 20 can be sleep or relaxation content. In the daytime, you can have Elton John and Harry Potter. It also means your favourites are there wherever you go, which is really good for holidays. We still love cards, though. In all our research, they’re still the main way younger kids want to use it.

For one of the players, up to 10 to 15 concepts across a few different areas. When we gave the more pebbly form to some children, it was obvious how naturally it fitted their hands and how much they wanted to hold on to it, so we presented that one with a strong recommendation. For the other, we looked at five or six directions, but Yoto wanted it to feel like a continuation of the previous products. The concept was quite singular, and we spent a lot of time on the detailing: where the dials sit, how sharp they should be, and so on.

What did you change about the dials and finish?

The dials used to be crisp. We softened them so kids can reach them from different angles, and made them slightly longer for more grip. The smart button isn’t in the middle, which most designers would do. Because it’s a kids’ product, kids can use it from the front as they hold it.

How do you work with such an opinionated community?

Because we’re external to Yoto, they do most of the community work and the feedback is funnelled to us through the Yoto team. We’re forthright about what we think is right within Yoto’s mission, and we don’t try to do everything people ask for. The challenge is that the community is always ageing up, but we also have to look after new families who’ve never used Yoto. A new user shouldn’t have to learn anything, and an existing user shouldn’t be thrown off because every feature suddenly does something else. The community’s feedback is great because it comes from hard-won experience, not assumptions.

By keeping the mischief, fun and wonder, and the underdog spirit, rather than suddenly feeling like a big corporation. My favourite bits are the hidden details. There are little faces between the dials, and the charging cable has four tiny Yoto logos, one of which is winking. No one’s going to talk about it, but one day someone will spot it and get a little flutter of appreciation.

#9047. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#9046. Dezeen Awards trophy updated using "one of humanity's oldest natural materials"

Photography courtesy of Corticeira Amorim

Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim has used sustainably harvested cork to refresh the latest edition of Dezeen’s iconic D-shaped trophy.

The trophies will be presented to this year’s winners at the Dezeen Awards party next week on 16 November at London’s Royal Opera House.

The event will bring together shortlisted studios, judges and the international architecture and design community to celebrate this year’s projects and reveal the 2026 winners, who will be the first to collect the new trophies.

Final tickets are available until 12pm London time on 11 November. Secure yours now.

An all-cork refresh for Dezeen Awards trophies

This year’s trophies have been produced in partnership with Corticeira Amorim, the world’s largest cork processing group, and mark the next material chapter for Dezeen’s trophy designs.

The updated design features an all-cork material palette that creates “a very direct encounter with the material”, according to Corticeira Amorim board member Cristina Amorim.

The group began by considering the trophy’s original design by Dutch studio Atelier NL, which was first created in 2018 and made from clay.

“The starting point was to preserve the recognisable form and graphic identity of the Dezeen Awards trophy, while allowing cork itself to become part of the design,” Amorim explained.

Cork is derived from the outer bark of the cork oak, which grows mainly in western Mediterranean countries such as Portugal, where Corticeira Amorim is based and has operated for over 150 years.

The material is renewable and recyclable. It is harvested without felling the tree, which naturally regenerates its bark to be harvested again at intervals of at least nine years.

Cork can also sequester carbon while replacing other, more polluting materials.

Beyond its sustainability credentials, the material is also remarkably light, resilient and adaptable in its nature.

“There is an interesting challenge in cork – it is one of humanity’s oldest natural materials, yet we are still discovering what it can do,” Amorim said.

This challenge spurred the development of different cork compositions, textures and finishes, after which a set of grains and colour references were selected to distinguish winner tiers while keeping a consistent visual language across the collection.

The winners of this year’s project categories, project of the year and Designers of the Year will each receive one of the bespoke cork trophies.

The project marks a continuation of Corticeira Amorim’s collaboration with architecture and design initiatives, revealing what Amorim sees as the “side of cork people may not expect”.

In 2024, the cork manufacturer produced the installations for City Cortex, a major arts programme that took place across the city of Lisbon.

The programme brought together internationally recognised architects and designers to create cork-based interventions for public and semi-public spaces, including Eduardo Souto de Moura, Diller Scofidio + Renfro and Yves Béhar.

Other notable projects also include Herzog & de Meuron and Ai Weiwei’s sunken 2012 Serpentine Pavilion, as well as product collaborations with designers including Jasper Morrison, the Bouroullecs and Naoto Fukasawa, showcasing the material’s broad potential.

“What makes cork surprising is its versatility: the same natural material can be transformed in so many different ways – some of them still unconceived,” Amorim said.

Reflecting on this year’s trophies, Amorim said: “cork is not simply associated with the awards – it becomes part of the award itself.”

“What we like about the final result is its simplicity,” she continued.

“The shape belongs unmistakably to the Dezeen Awards, but the texture, warmth, grain and natural variation belong unmistakably to cork.”

Previous editions of the Dezeen Awards trophy have explored materials including a compound of micro-paper, wood from London street trees and clay used to make the traditional yellow bricks found in the UK’s capital.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

Photography courtesy of Corticeira Amorim

#9045. inside the mercedes-benz SLR mclaren stirling moss, a supercar built without a windshield

with an elongated hood and no windshield, the speedster revisits the dramatic proportions of 1950s racing cars.

The Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss is a rare sight, especially in this bright Fire Opal Red finish. Built in a series of just 75 cars, the unusual two-seater has an exceptionally long hood, a low body, and an open cockpit with neither a roof nor a conventional windshield. Two sculpted humps rise behind the seats to give the car a profile that recalls the racing machines of the 1950s.

Mercedes-Benz and McLaren introduced the Stirling Moss in 2009 as a tribute to British racing driver Stirling Moss and the Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR he drove to victory in the 1955 Mille Miglia. The original was a lightweight, open-top race car built to compete on public roads through Italy. More than half a century later, its distinctive design inspired this modern interpretation, developed toward the end of the Mercedes-Benz and McLaren partnership. RM Sotheby’s is auctioning the speedster, with an estimate exceeding 6 million USD.

Much of the Stirling Moss’s character comes from its proportions. The hood stretches far ahead of the two seats, while the rear of the car is relatively short. Small transparent wind deflectors offer some protection for the occupants, and the raised forms behind their heads incorporate protective roll hoops. Viewed from the side, the entire car sits ultra-close to the ground.

There are plenty of details to discover along the bodywork, too. Large openings behind the front wheels house the exhaust outlets, which release gases directly from the sides of the car. Its doors open upward, while the front is shaped around a low Mercedes-Benz emblem and wide air intakes. Much of the body is made from carbon fiber, which helps to keep the car lightweight despite its substantial length.

Under the enormous hood lurks a supercharged 5.4-liter V8 engine producing 650 horsepower. That’s enough to send the Stirling Moss from zero to 62 mph in under 3.5 seconds, with a top speed of 217 mph. Without a full windshield separating the driver from the outside air, the experience would be especially intense. The small wind deflectors and exposed seating position are part of the car’s connection to its racing predecessor.

Inside, the two red leather seats are divided by a tall silver center console, with matching red trim extending across the dashboard. Yellow stitching adds a contrasting detail to the seats, while the steering wheel and circular air vents are familiar from other Mercedes-Benz models of the period. The open cockpit also makes the interior unusually visible from outside, so its colors and materials become part of the overall design.

This particular Stirling Moss is the very last of the 75 examples produced, completed in December 2009 for the Royal Family of Kuwait. Its Fire Opal Red paint is unique among the series, whose silver examples are more closely associated with the Mercedes-Benz racing tradition. The matching red interior features a woven material called Alutex in place of the usual carbon fiber trim, along with a rare Kenwood audio system.

After spending much of its life in royal ownership, the car has now resurfaced through RM Sotheby’s, showing just 32.9 miles on its odometer. Its estimated value exceeds $6 million. Even among today’s increasingly elaborate supercars, the Stirling Moss remains an unusual piece of automotive design, with its roofless silhouette and distinctive twin humps drawing directly from a racing car built more than 70 years ago.

This may be the best stoopid idea for a Christmas gift I’ve seen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Struggling to find a Christmas or Black Friday prezzie for the person who owns every novelty mug on Earth? Why not gift a palm-sized robot programmed to endure a relentless existential crisis on your desk?! Ladies and gentlemen – here is the Butter Bot.

Following a successful 2024 Kickstarter and two years of intensive engineering, creative tech studio CircuitMess is finally shipping its officially licensed Rick and Morty Butter Bot. And yes, theoretically, it will be able to pass you the butter. Better yet, it rolls around on rubber caterpillar tracks delivering deadpan commentary about the futility of its own existence. Yes please!

However, even though this grumpy little companion looks like the product of some of the best 3D printers out there, it will set you back $349. Yeah, it's for the ultra-fans only.

Inspired by a two-second gag from the intro of an Rick and Morty episode, Butter Bot started life as a cult Kickstarter project backed by 2,715 eager fans ($441,349 pledged). CircuitMess spent two years, and three electronics revisions plus custom steel moulds, turning that animated gag into a real, palm-sized AI desk robot.

And yes, of course this includes AI. Under the hood, it packs an onboard AI camera, dual microphones, edge sensors, and a remote controller featuring a live first-person video feed. Because its voice, face, and object recognition run on-device, it should recognise its owner, identify random desk clutter, read out phone notifications, tell jokes, control your TV, and – crucially – ferry sticks of butter across the table (though how the hell this is done is currently a mystery to me).

Left alone, it roams your workspace, avoids table edges, and loudly questions its own purpose. Pick it up and it panics; shake it and it disapproves; press the controller’s 'Poke' button and you’ll visibly irritate it.

Tinkerers can also snap on six modular add-ons, including an air-quality sensor, motion-sensing intruder alarm, and LED light show. O you can reprogram its open-source brain from scratch using C++ or CircuitBlocks (I'll leave that to the people in the know).

Available worldwide now at circuitmess.com for $349, it’s a wonderfully over-engineered piece of pop-culture hardware that can turn existential dread into festive cheer. If you can afford it!

#9042. Gustaf Westman unveils full Disney collection featuring Donald Duck bookstand and Pluto mirror

Swedish designer Gustaf Westman‘s full collaboration with media company Disney, which saw him reimagine familiar Disney details “through his own design language”, has been revealed.

The collection, which launches on 15 November, features homeware, accessories and glassware, alongside made-to-order furniture.

Among the furniture pieces are a bookstand designed to resemble Donald Duck, a Goofy coffee table and Mickey dresser, as well as a Pluto mirror.

Each takes recognisable features from the Disney characters and turns them into parts of the design object, with the Donald bookstand decorated with his hat and duck feet.

Westman told Dezeen he wanted to work with Disney because he grew up with the brand.

“Disney is part of so many people’s childhood, including mine,” the designer explained.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” he continued.

His aim was to create something new while using details that are deeply familiar to many.

“I wanted to take those familiar details and reimagine them through my own design language, with sculptural, playful forms in bold proportions, and bring that sense of joy into people’s homes,” Westman said.

The collection also includes smaller objects such as a vase designed to look like Mickey’s trousers, a glass that evokes Minnie Mouse and a candelabra resembling Donald Duck.

There is also merch, including a T-shirt, hoodie, keychains, hairbands and pins.

Westman’s own favourite object is the Mickey Tumbler, which was one of the first objects from the collection to be revealed.

“The Mickey Tumbler is my favourite,” he said.

“It combines my chunky shapes with Mickey’s signature colours and an ear-shaped lid, so both worlds are instantly recognisable without overcomplicating the design.”

Disney and Westman are hosting a series of pop-up experiences in Tokyo, New York and Paris to launch the collection before it is released online.

Disney also targeted the homeware and interior industries in 2022, when it launched its own homeware brand.

#9041. Dezeen Awards-shortlisted housing project damaged in fire

Photography and video by Andorran Police unless otherwise stated

A fire has damaged the La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Located in the valley of Ordino, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote.

According to Andorran Police, officials were warned at 01:45 on 22 September about the fire, which spread to all seven buildings in the uninhabited development, affecting 10,000 square metres of housing.

The cause of the fire remains unknown, reported local newspaper La Veu Lliure. No official estimate of the damage has been released, and a date for reconstruction to commence has not yet been announced.

La Querola was completed in October 2025 but had not been occupied. Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos designed the housing to appear as if emerging from the natural landscape, with an angular exterior that evokes stratified, eroded rock.

The housing is made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley.

“The client’s brief called for a residential development within a landscape of exceptional natural value, a context in which any construction inevitably enters into dialogue with a protected mountain environment,” said Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos when entering the housing into the Dezeen Awards.

“The built volume is modelled as a fragmented, stratified mass, avoiding repetitive or generic gestures in favour of a form that reads as eroded geology.”

Clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

Duplex and triplex apartments were designed to have views of the surrounding valley, with wood lining the interior surfaces to add a sense of warmth.

“Voids and cavities pierce the volume, structuring the relationship between built mass and open territory, and generating terraces that function as habitable extensions of the building’s body,” said Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

“Openings are conceived not as conventional windows but as deep incisions and habitable cavities – spaces of varying depth that are occupied by fireplaces, bathtubs and other domestic fixtures, making the thickness of the envelope a place in its own right and allowing the geography to penetrate the deepest corners of the interior.”

Other buildings that have been shortlisted in this year’s Dezeen Awards include an off-grid home in Japan topped with a large metal roof and a renovated house in Japan with walls streaked in clay, soil and metal powders.

#9039. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#9038. marlot meyer’s giant inflatable creatures breathe with the tides of the wadden sea

inspired by microscopic algae, these breathing sculptures translate tidal movements into an interactive experience.

Inside an Amsterdam gallery, Dutch artist Marlot Meyer’s Pneuma (2025) brings together a curious population of giant inflatable creatures. Some tower above visitors, their brightly colored bodies swelling and shrinking as though they were breathing. Their movements follow the tides of the Wadden Sea along the Dutch coast, while visitors can influence the sculptures through their own breath.

The interactive installation connects two rhythms that operate on very different scales. This way, the movement of an entire coastal ecosystem becomes something people can experience through their own bodies.

Visitors are invited to embrace smaller inflatable beings fitted to the body with sensors that register their own breathing. These signals are translated into movements within the larger sculptures, creating a strange exchange between human respiration and the movements of the sea. The creatures appear to have lives of their own, responding to a distant environment while remaining sensitive to the people around them.

Before developing Pneuma, artist Marlot Meyer spent three months in Friesland, in the northern Netherlands, investigating whether humans could learn to physically sense the changing tides. During her residency at Het Lage Noorden, she placed wetness sensors in the mudflats near the Wadden Sea, which transmitted environmental data through radio signals to wearable devices. She called this research Project Tidal. Her aim was to introduce a new kind of sensory awareness, allowing the body to recognize the movement of water without having to see it.

Early experiments used small vibrating motors worn against the skin, with changes in the water translated into different vibrations. Meyer eventually began working with inflatable wearables, which she felt offered a more natural interpretation of the sea’s gradual movement. As water levels rose, an air-filled device would expand against her abdomen, creating pressure that would ease as the tide retreated.

The sensation was intended to become familiar over time, perhaps allowing the body’s own awareness to extend into the surrounding landscape.

The research proved to be unpredictable. Sensors lost their connection, batteries failed, and changing conditions made it difficult to collect consistent information. At one point, an especially powerful spring tide submerged Meyer’s equipment, which flooded the electronics and interrupted weeks of recordings. The experience brought her back to the very quality of the sea she had been trying to capture: its constant movement and resistance to control.

In her research journal, the artist reflects on the tension between technological precision and the experience of being in an environment that continually changes. ‘How to find the balance between information and meaning?‘ she asks. The question became central to the development of Pneuma, as the project gradually moved beyond the collection of tidal data toward finding ways to experience it.

the higher the tide, the more wet the land is, the more pressure is pumped into the inflatable

The unusual forms of Pneuma take inspiration from diatoms, microscopic algae that Meyer encountered in the Wadden Sea’s muddy sediment. These tiny organisms respond to tidal cycles, moving deeper into the mud as water rises and returning toward the surface when conditions allow them to capture sunlight. Some species can maintain their internal tidal rhythms even when removed from their natural environment.

Diatoms play an important role in marine ecosystems, supporting food webs through photosynthesis. Their intricate cell walls, made from silica, give them surprisingly elaborate shapes when viewed under a microscope. Meyer translates these tiny organisms into oversized, bulbous sculptures, with rounded protrusions and brightly colored surfaces. Enlarged to the scale of the human body, creatures that ordinarily go unseen become the dominant inhabitants of the room.

The title Pneuma comes from the ancient Greek word for both breath and spirit. In the installation, breathing becomes a way to participate in an environmental rhythm that continues well beyond the gallery. A visitor’s breath can change the shape of an inflatable creature, while the tides influence the same sculptural environment at their own pace.

Meyer’s work proposes an interesting possibility for how we might relate to the natural world. We already use technology to monitor environmental changes, usually translating them into numbers and graphs. Pneuma brings that information into the body by exploring whether physical sensation can create a more immediate relationship with forces that normally escape our perception.

The installation leaves viewers with a curious question: if we could learn to feel the movement of the sea, would we begin to experience our place within the environment differently?

the bulbous sculptures take inspiration from microscopic algae known as diatomssensors translate human respiration into movements within the larger inflatable forms
